cim: USF receives grant to create AI and cyber makerspace
cim_eredeti: USF receives grant to create AI and cyber makerspace
szoveg_eredeti:
University of South Florida leaders believe that a hands-on approach is essential for education, especially when it comes to emerging technologies.

Last week, the institution announced that it has received a $2 million grant from the National Institute of Standards and Technology to create an Artificial Intelligence and Cyber Makerspace.

The facility will be located in the future Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing building on the Tampa campus. The college was established with a $40 million gift from Arnie Bellini, co-founder of Tampa-based software company ConnectWise, and his wife Lauren. A timeline for construction has not been disclosed. However, a temporary lab is currently in development.

“It’s a place where students can come and experiment,” said Sudeep Sarkar, launch dean of the Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing. “We plan to design a space that can be used for different courses and labs. We have identified a set of courses and there’s about 800 students who can potentially use that space.”

He believes that firsthand experience will make learners more marketable and could open doors to more internship and job opportunities.

Sudeep Sarkar is the launch dean of the Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing. Photo provided.

The makerspace will support advanced computing, hardware experimentation and secure data research, according to USF’s website. Additionally, it will be used for laboratory instruction in networking, embedded systems, microcontroller design, hardware and software reverse engineering and vulnerability analysis.

For example, Sarkar explained that students will get to explore edge AI, which runs on local physical devices (such as sensors and cameras). This will help them learn how to create low power AI hardware that does not rely on centralized cloud facilities.

There will be a variety of equipment for learners to utilize. Currently, USF leaders are having conversations with faculty and industry professionals to determine what products should be acquired.

“I’m also hoping that the students can experiment with things in a safe environment,” added Richard Rauscher, associate professor of instruction at the Bellini College and assistant dean of computing. “I’d like to give students an opportunity to kind of play with those things in a place that’s sealed off from the real universe a little bit.”

Richard Rauscher is an associate professor of instruction at the Bellini College and the assistant dean of computing. Photo provided.

USF leaders plan to make the facility available to regional businesses and public sector organizations. This will allow professionals to explore AI applications as well as security risks, according to USF’s website.

“AI is a technology that’s here to stay,” Sarkar explained. “We can look the other way and ignore it or we can wrestle it and bring it down to the ground and use it. I think we need to create a workforce that is able to wrestle the technology down.”

Rauscher believes that the tool is changing the world in a profound way. Additionally, many individuals and organizations are exploring AI.

“Whether that investment will sustain and how that will fluctuate over time, we’ll find out as time goes on,” he said. “So, we want to prepare our students for that change to help them be as well-tooled as possible so they can go out and get rewarding jobs.”

Sarkar emphasized that these young people will ultimately shape the future of AI. They will research the technology’s issues and find solutions.
